results.conclusion: The yen's recent move is a reminder that currency markets can turn quickly, especially when they are positioned one way. The rate differential remains the dominant driver, but it is not the only one. I will be watching the data, the rhetoric from the BoJ and the Fed, and the positioning of carry traders. As always, I will try to separate what is said and what gets done. That distinction has served me well in the past, and I suspect it will continue to do so. For now, I am keeping an open mind. The yen could strengthen further if the BoJ signals a policy shift, or it could weaken if the Fed delays rate cuts. Either way, investors should be prepared for volatility. That is not a prediction; it is a recognition of uncertainty. And in my experience, acknowledging uncertainty is the first step toward managing it. Speaking as an ex-central banker, I've learned to be wary of drawing firm conclusions from short stretches of market action. The yen has strengthened against the dollar in recent weeks, and that move has prompted a familiar debate about whether the long-standing rate differential between Japan and the United States is finally narrowing in a way that matters for investors. I want to separate what has been said by officials from what markets have actually done, because the two are not always aligned. First, the facts as I read them. The Federal Reserve has held its policy rate in a range that is high by the standards of the past decade, while the Bank of Japan has kept its short-term policy rate negative and continues to cap long-term yields through its yield curve control framework. That configuration has been the anchor for the yen carry trade, in which investors borrow in yen and invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere. The carry trade has been profitable for a long time, but it is not without risk, as the sharp unwinding episodes of the past have shown. The Bank of Japan has repeatedly indicated that it won't hesitate to ease further if needed, but it has also acknowledged that the side effects of prolonged easing are becoming more visible. In its most recent statements, the bank has emphasized the importance of wage growth and inflation expectations in determining the future path of policy. Governor Ueda has said that the bank will carefully assess the data before making any changes, and that it does not target the exchange rate. That is a standard line, but it is worth taking at face value: the BoJ's mandate is price stability, not a particular yen level. At the same time, there have been hints that the bank is thinking about the sustainability of its framework. The yield curve control policy has been tweaked several times to allow long-term rates to move more flexibly, and each tweak has been interpreted by markets as a step toward normalization. But the bank has been careful to frame these moves as technical adjustments, not as a change in the overall stance of monetary policy. I think that is the right way to read them. Markets, however, have a habit of running ahead of central banks. The yen's recent appreciation has been driven in part by expectations that the rate differential will narrow, either because the Fed will cut rates or because the BoJ will raise them. But the actual differential remains wide. The 10-year US Treasury yield is still well above the 10-year JGB yield, even after the recent moves. That gap is the compensation for currency risk, and it is why the carry trade persists. I have seen some commentary suggesting that the yen's move is a sign that the carry trade is dead. I am not convinced. Carry trades have a tendency to revive when volatility subsides, and the underlying differential is still substantial. What has changed is that the market is now more alert to the risk of a policy shift. That means the carry trade is likely to be more volatile, with sharper unwinds when data surprises. For investors, that is a reason to size positions carefully and to consider hedging currency risk more actively.

results.question: Which Singapore banks offer the highest fixed deposit rate this month?
results.conclusion: And why would you refinance? Because the paperwork is a nightmare, the legal fees are annoying, and your existing bank will offer you a "loyalty" spread that is only slightly worse than a kick in the teeth. So you stay. You grumble. You pay. The bank sends you a mooncake every Chinese New Year and considers the relationship healthy. I tried to refinance once. I spent three weeks gathering documents, only to be told that my loan-to-value ratio had crept up because the property next door sold for less than expected. The bank offered me a rate that was higher than my existing one, then acted like they were doing me a favour. I walked away. I am still walking. I have a confession: I love Singapore. The food, the efficiency, the way the MRT actually works. But the way this island treats home loans is a masterclass in collective denial. Everyone I know is fixated on the property price, the stamp duty, the renovation budget. Nobody talks about the interest rate. It is the elephant in the room, except the elephant is wearing a nice suit and quietly raising your monthly instalment while you admire the view from your 30th-floor condo. Here is the thing. For years, rates were so low that a mortgage felt like a rounding error. You signed the papers, the banker smiled, and you went back to scrolling PropertyGuru. But rates do not stay low forever. They never do. And when they move, they move fast, like a taxi driver who just saw a green light. The problem is that Singapore's home loan market is structurally allergic to rate rises, and almost nobody is prepared. Let me be blunt: most "fixed rate" packages in Singapore are fixed for about as long as a New Year's resolution. Two years, maybe three, then you are dumped into a floating rate that tracks SORA or some bank's internal board rate, which is a polite way of saying "whatever we feel like." The banks know this. They price the fixed period as a loss leader, then make it back when you are too lazy or too busy to refinance. If you have a floating rate loan, stress-test it. Imagine your monthly payment going up by 50 percent. Can you still afford it? If not, fix it now, even if the fixed rate looks ugly. Ugly and predictable beats pretty and volatile. And if you are thinking of buying, factor in the rate rise that is almost certainly coming. The seller's agent will not mention it. The bank will not mention it. But it is there, lurking, like a durian on a hot day. The 10-year JGB yield closed at 2.05% on 17 September 2026, 2.14% on 18 September 2026 (+9 bp) and 2.19% on 22 September 2026, according to closing quotes published by the Japan Bond Trading Co. and cross-checked against data from the Ministry of Finance. The 18 September move represented the largest single-session increase in the benchmark tenor since the Bank of Japan exited its negative-rate policy in March 2024. Trading volumes on 18 September were reported at 2.4 trillion yen in the when-issued and on-the-run 10-year sector, compared with a 30-day average of 1.8 trillion yen. The 22 September close extended the rise, with the yield touching an intraday high of 2.21% before settling at 2.19%. No unscheduled operations were announced by the Bank of Japan on either date. The Bank of Japan conducted its regular outright purchase operations for 5-year to 10-year JGBs on 18 September 2026, offering to buy 600 billion yen at fixed-rate and variable-rate auctions. The operation was oversubscribed by a factor of 2.1. On 19 September 2026, the Bank of Japan released its quarterly outlook report, which stated that long-term interest rates would be allowed to "move more flexibly" in response to economic and price conditions. The report did not specify a target range for the 10-year yield. The next Monetary Policy Meeting is scheduled for 28-29 October 2026. Minutes from the September meeting, released on 25 September 2026, showed that seven members voted to raise the policy rate by 25 bp to 1.00%, while two members preferred to keep it at 0.75%.

results.question: What are the best things to do in Tokyo in spring?
results.conclusion: Something is moving in Tokyo, and it is not the Nikkei. I have been sitting on this for weeks, waiting for the right moment, and that moment is now. People familiar with the matter tell me that the bidding behavior at recent Japanese government bond auctions has shifted in ways that seasoned desks are only beginning to whisper about. Nobody wants to say it on the record. Nobody ever does. But the tape does not lie, and the people who watch the tape for a living are suddenly very, very interested in what the Ministry of Finance is doing behind closed doors. The problem is simple to state and impossible to solve. If the BoJ steps back, the long end has to clear at a price that nobody wants to pay. If the BoJ steps in, it doubles down on a balance sheet that is already the size of a small continent's economy. There is no third option. There has never been a third option. The only question is which version of the impossible they choose, and when they choose it. The window here is not wide. The auctions are coming, the announcements are coming, and the repricing is coming. The only question is whether you are positioned before or after. I know which side I would rather be on. I am not going to tell you which side that is, because that is what the paid tier is for. But I will say this: the whispers are getting louder, and the people doing the whispering are not the kind who whisper for fun. Here is where it gets interesting. The people I talk to, and I talk to people who would lose their jobs if their names appeared anywhere near this article, say the composition of buyers at the long end has changed in a way that is not yet visible in the headline coverage. The usual suspects are still showing up. But the size of their tickets, and the timing of their entries, tells a different story than the one being sold to the public. One source, who has been trading JGBs since before most of you were born, described the current environment as "the most interesting setup in a generation." That is not a phrase people use lightly in this market. This is a market where "interesting" usually means "nothing happened, but slowly." Now the same people are using words like "regime change" and "inflection point." I am not making this up. I wish I were, because it would make my life easier. The Bank of Japan, for its part, continues to do what the Bank of Japan does, which is to say one thing and do another, and then deny that either thing happened. But the people familiar with the auction calendar know that the rhythm has changed. The spacing between operations is not what it was. The maturity mix is not what it was. And the primary dealers, who are contractually obligated to show up and bid, are showing up with a different attitude. That attitude is the story. Let us talk about the elephant in the room, which is the Bank of Japan itself. The central bank has spent years doing things that textbooks say are impossible, and it has gotten away with it because the world was willing to look the other way. That willingness is now being tested. People close to the situation tell me that the internal debates at the BoJ have become, in the words of one person, "lively." That is central banker for "we are arguing about everything." And here is the part that should make you sit up. The people I talk to say the decision has already been made. Not announced. Not leaked. Made. The auctions are the tell. If you know what to look for, the bids are already voting. I am not going to spell it out for you in this paragraph, because the people who need to know already know, and the people who do not need to know will find out the hard way.
